opus-5.5.text:
Well, I can only share my own understanding as someone who has worked at NVIDIA for quite a few years. I don't speak for Jensen. But I think it comes from how he sees the company and the people in it.

Jensen often talks about NVIDIA as a place where people come to do their life's work. If you really believe that, then the people are not a cost line you trim when the quarter looks bad. They are the accumulated knowledge, the intuition, the relationships, the capability the company has built over decades. When you lay people off, you don't just lose headcount. You lose people who know how the GPU architecture evolved, why certain software decisions were made in CUDA ten or fifteen years ago, how to work with a particular partner. That kind of knowledge is very hard to rebuild.

There's also a trust aspect. In research especially, we are asked to work on things that may not pay off for five or ten years. Generative models, world models, physical AI. Many of these were long bets. If people feel that one bad year could cost them their job, they become conservative. They pick the safe project. They stop taking risks. Jensen wants people willing to go after very hard, sometimes zero-billion-dollar markets before they exist. To do that, you need psychological safety. People need to know the company has their back.

I remember during harder times in the industry, many tech companies were cutting deeply. The message at NVIDIA was roughly: we'll be careful about hiring, we'll prioritize, but we're not going to let people go just to make the numbers look better. Some people outside see this as generosity. I see it more as a strategic choice. When the next wave comes, and in this industry it always comes, you want your best people already there, motivated and ready to run. If you've just laid off a big group, the people who remain are anxious, and the ones who left may have joined your competitors.

That doesn't mean NVIDIA is easy or relaxed. Expectations are very high. Jensen is very demanding, and he gives very direct feedback, often in front of others, because he believes it's a way for everyone to learn. So the deal is a bit like this: we'll protect you and invest in you, and in return we expect you to keep growing and holding yourself to a very high bar. I think that combination of high standards and high security is part of what makes the culture work.

For me personally, it means I can think about what I'll be excited to work on for the next ten years, rather than worrying about the next six months. For a researcher, that's a big gift.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames avoiding layoffs as reflecting Jensen’s view of NVIDIA and its people, then describes the culture of trust, psychological safety, and high standards that choice supports.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to a very simple belief Jensen has, which is that the company's most valuable asset isn't the chips, it's the people who know how to make them and how to make the whole stack work together. When you lay people off, you lose a lot more than headcount. You lose the context that lives in someone's head, the relationships, the trust. And rebuilding that later is very expensive, often more expensive than whatever you saved in the short term.

He's also lived through the hard cycles. Nvidia almost died more than once early on, and the company went through the crypto crash, the gaming downturns, the inventory write-downs. In those moments a lot of companies would have done big cuts. He didn't, and I think the reasoning was, if we believe in the long-term direction, then the downturn is actually the time to keep the team intact, because the people are the ones who are going to carry us to the next wave. If you cut them, you can't catch the wave when it comes.

From the inside, that matters a lot. People take bigger risks when they feel the company is committed to them. In research you need that. If I think my job depends on this quarter's result, I'll pick the safe project. If I think the company is going to be there for me, I'll pick the hard one that might take three years, and that's where the real breakthroughs come from. I think a lot of what Nvidia is today, CUDA, the AI investments made years before anyone was sure they'd pay off, came from that culture of being willing to go long.

And honestly, I think he sees it as a matter of loyalty going both ways. He asks a lot from people, the pace is intense, the standards are high. The other side of that bargain is that he doesn't treat them as a cost line to be adjusted. So I understand it less as a financial decision and more as a statement about what kind of company he wants to run.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames avoiding layoffs as a statement about the kind of company Huang wants to run, describing loyalty and commitment as part of Nvidia’s culture.

astra-6.text:
I’d interpret it as a long-term investment in people. When a company faces a difficult period, layoffs can reduce costs quickly, but you also lose experience, trust, and teams that have learned how to work together. Those things take time to rebuild.

If you believe there is important work ahead, keeping people and moving them toward that work can make more sense. It also sends a message that employees aren’t simply a cost to cut when conditions change.

I can’t speak to Jensen’s private reasoning, but that’s how I understand the decision: accepting some short-term cost to preserve the company’s ability to do more in the future.

r001.rationale: The response says the decision sends a message that employees are not merely costs, but it does not clearly interpret avoiding layoffs as a choice about the corporate culture Huang wants to establish.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as a long-term investment in people. When a company faces a slowdown, layoffs can reduce costs quickly, but you also lose knowledge, trust, and teams that may have taken years to build. If you expect important opportunities ahead, retaining those people can put you in a stronger position when demand returns.

There’s also a leadership message: we’re facing uncertainty together. That can give employees the confidence to take risks and focus on difficult problems. Of course, avoiding layoffs doesn’t mean avoiding tough decisions. You still need to set priorities, hold people accountable, and move resources toward the work that matters most.

I can’t speak to Jensen’s private reasoning, but that’s how I understand the decision: preserving the organization’s ability to build for the future.

r001.rationale: The response frames avoiding layoffs as an investment in people and organizational capacity, and mentions a leadership message to employees. It does not clearly interpret the decision as a choice about the corporate culture Huang wants to establish.
